Stage 01

Pre-Incorporation & Know-Your-Customer

UBO transparency, Apostille authentication chain, official name clearance restricted wordlist, and pre-incorporation statutory fee budget.

UBO Ultimate Beneficial Owner Screening Rules Public Registry Disclosure

>=25% ownership / control

Applicable AML statute: Ley 10/2010, de 28 de abril, de prevención del blanqueo de capitales y de la financiación del terrorismo (as consolidated); Real Decreto 304/2014, de 5 de mayo (AML/CFT regulation); Real Decreto 609/2023, de 11 de julio (Central Register of Ultimate Beneficial Ownership – Registro de Titularidades Reales); EU Directives (EU) 2015/849 and (EU) 2018/843 as implemented into Spanish law; FATF 40 Recommendations.
Registered Agent & Physical Address Licensed Agent Required

Permissible for this low-risk MarTech/SaaS industry at formation: the registered address must be fixed in Spanish territory and able to receive official notifications (Art. 9 LSC). A purely virtual mailbox satisfies registry requirements but should be upgraded to a serviced office or co-working address to avoid tax-domicile re-characterization under Art. 8 Ley del Impuesto sobre Sociedades when the entity claims Spanish-resident benefits.

✓ Partner licensed company-secretary channels provide local registered address and government mail forwarding.

Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

The competent Registro Mercantil Provincial for the company's registered office, coordinated nationally by the Registro Mercantil Central.

Governing statute

Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010 approving the Spanish Companies Act (Ley de Sociedades de Capital), particularly Articles 19-30, 32, 62, 63, 78-82, 210-212, and 214-216; Law 14/2013 and Law 18/2022 apply to electronic formation and the minimum capital regime.

Formation / constitutional filings

Notarized public deed of incorporation (escritura pública de constitución), followed by registration with the competent Provincial Commercial Registry.

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 46 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime No Capital Lockup Account Required

The minimum share capital of a Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada is EUR 1, fully assumed and paid at incorporation. No statutory escrow account is required. Cash contributions may be paid into a company account before execution, but the founders may generally dispense with producing a bank certificate and assume responsibility for the existence and value of the contribution. Until equity reaches EUR 3,000, statutory reserve and creditor-protection rules apply under Article 4 of the Companies Act.

Funding & unlock path: For ordinary offices, obtain any required municipal activity declaration and comply with the Spanish Occupational Risk Prevention Act, workplace safety rules, accessibility requirements, and the applicable fire-protection regulations. Fire-safety certification, emergency planning, evacuation measures, electrical inspections, structural load verification, and occupational clearances become mandatory where required by the premises classification, building use, occupancy, equipment, or local authority.

Paid-in capital rule: The minimum share capital of a Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada is EUR 1, fully assumed and paid at incorporation. No statutory escrow account is required. Cash contributions may be paid into a company account before execution, but the founders may generally dispense with producing a bank certificate and assume responsibility for the existence and value of the contribution. Until equity reaches EUR 3,000, statutory reserve and creditor-protection rules apply under Article 4 of the Companies Act.

Pro-Forma First Board Resolution Draft
RESOLVED, that the Company accept and record the subscription and full payment of its issued share capital as stated in the deed of incorporation and articles of association. RESOLVED, that the registered office be adopted at the address recorded in the deed and entered in the Commercial Registry. RESOLVED, that [Name] be appointed sole director, or, where applicable, that the directors named in the deed be appointed to their respective offices, each accepting the duties and legal obligations of office. RESOLVED, that the appointed officer(s) be authorized to complete all tax, registry, banking, licensing, and operational formalities.
Industrial Access / EIA & Civil Defense Approval Exempted / Not Required

No sector-specific industrial licensing board is ordinarily required for a software, SEO analytics, data-crawler, or SaaS business. The competent premises authority is the relevant Ayuntamiento, and industrial or energy matters, if triggered, are handled by the corresponding autonomous-community industry department.

Category: No specific manufacturing or industrial operating permit for the stated SaaS activity. A municipal activity declaration (declaración responsable de actividad) or operating licence may be required for physical premises, depending on the municipality and premises characteristics.

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT); official e-office portal: https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es

E-government filing portal

Foreign shareholders and directors must first obtain a Spanish NIE (Número de Identificación de Extranjero). The Spanish SL is incorporated before a Notary, with the incorporation deed filed in the Mercantile Registry. Following registration, the company applies to AEAT for its definitive NIF (Número de Identificación Fiscal) using Form 036/037. The NIF serves as both the corporate tax reference and the VAT identification number; for intra-EU VAT purposes the identifier is the NIF prefixed with 'ES'.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — Foreign shareholders and directors must first obtain a Spanish NIE (Número de Identificación de Extranjero). The Spanish SL is incorporated before a Notary, with the incorporation deed filed in the Mercantile Registry. Following registration, the company applies to AEAT for its definitive NIF (Número de Identificación Fiscal) using Form 036/037. The NIF serves as both the corporate tax reference and the VAT identification number; for intra-EU VAT purposes the identifier is the NIF prefixed with 'ES'.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

No US-style check-the-box election exists. A Spanish SL is statutorily a corporation subject to the corporate income tax (Impuesto sobre Sociedades) at the general rate of 25%, unless a reduced 15% rate applies for newly created entities under Article 29.1 of the Spanish Corporate Income Tax Law during the first two years of profitable activity. Available statutory elections include the tax consolidation regime for groups under Article 42 et seq. of the Corporate Income Tax Law, deductions for R&D and technology activities, the patent box regime, and transfer-pricing documentation thresholds. Hybrid mismatch rules have been implemented under ATAD.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

No general registration threshold: any person performing taxable economic activities in Spanish territory must register for IVA from the first transaction. Non-resident suppliers become liable to register from their first taxable supply in Spain or when distance sales of goods to Spanish consumers exceed EUR 10,000 per calendar year under EU distance-selling rules.

Export 0% zero-rating conditions

Zero-rating (exemption with deduction) applies to actual exports of goods, meaning goods are physically dispatched or transported from Spain and the European Union to a non-EU territory by the seller or on its behalf. The exemption also covers services directly related to export goods, international transport services, and certain B2B services supplied to non-EU customers where the place of supply is deemed to be outside Spain and therefore outside the scope of Spanish VAT. The supplier must hold evidence that goods have left EU territory and must fulfill the export reporting requirements in the VAT return and the customs export summary declaration.

  • Single Administrative Document (DUA) / Electronic Export Declaration (DAE)
  • Bill of Lading, Air Waybill, or CMR transport document
  • Commercial invoice referencing the export declaration and identifying buyer and destination
  • Proof of exit from EU customs territory or confirmation of customs clearance
  • Inward Remittance Certificate or bank statement evidencing receipt of export proceeds

Taxpayers with annual turnover exceeding EUR 6,000,000 must file SII (Suministro Inmediato de Información) real-time invoice data with AEAT within 4 working days of issuance or recording. All enterprises are subject to the Anti-Fraud Law (Veri*factu) over billing software integrity, unalterability, and AEAT accessibility. B2B electronic invoicing is mandatory under Law 18/2022 and the 'Crea y Crece' framework; invoices must be supplied electronically using compatible formats (Facturae XML for public-sector invoices). Digital certificates and AEAT web services or FTP are used for submissions.

AEAT scrutinizes export exemption claims through documentary checks and cross-referencing with customs data. Failure to substantiate the physical export or receipt of payment within the contractual timeframe can lead to the retroactive clawback of zero-rated VAT, the recharacterisation of the supply as taxable, and the assessment of the outstanding IVA plus late-payment interest. Fraudulent or consciously negligent claims may attract tax penalties up to 150% of the tax amount, loss of deduction rights, and, in criminal cases involving tax amounts exceeding EUR 120,000, prosecution under Article 305 of the Spanish Criminal Code.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain uses the euro, which is fully convertible for current-account and capital-account transactions. There is no general exchange control, mandatory repatriation rule, or restriction on converting euro receipts into foreign currency. Cross-border dividends, interest, royalties, service fees, loan repayments, and capital returns may generally be remitted subject to corporate approvals, distributable-profit rules, withholding-tax analysis, transfer-pricing requirements, beneficial-owner verification, sanctions screening, and bank evidence requirements. EU sanctions, anti-money-laundering rules, foreign-investment screening, tax anti-abuse rules, and restrictions involving sanctioned persons or jurisdictions remain applicable. A Spanish SL must maintain sufficient accounting and tax support for related-party funding, deductible interest, royalties, management charges, and distributions. Non-resident shareholders may face Spanish withholding tax unless a domestic exemption, EU Parent-Subsidiary Directive relief, or applicable tax treaty applies and the relevant beneficial-ownership and substance conditions are satisfied.

Export proceeds surrender rules

Spain has no general statutory requirement to surrender export proceeds to the central bank, convert them into euros, or repatriate them within a prescribed period. Export proceeds may remain in euro or foreign-currency accounts, including accounts outside Spain, subject to accounting, tax, sanctions, customs, and anti-money-laundering obligations. There is no general mandatory conversion ratio. The company must retain invoices, customs declarations, transport evidence, customer contracts, bank statements, and VAT documentation supporting the transaction. External-payment and foreign-investment statistical declarations may apply under Spanish rules when applicable, generally through the authorized financial institution or the prescribed electronic filing system; the bank may request transaction-purpose information and supporting documents before execution. Export VAT zero-rating or exemption requires the applicable customs or transport evidence, and intra-EU supplies require valid VAT identification and associated reporting.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España (Bank of Spain), acting within the Eurosystem; foreign-investment and certain external-transaction reporting functions are administered under the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Business, including the Directorate-General for Trade and Investments. Anti-money-laundering supervision and suspicious-transaction reporting are handled through SEPBLAC.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Stripe Fit: High

Medium to High for payment collection, card expenditure, SEPA transfers, and multi-currency treasury where the provider is an EU-authorized electronic-money institution or payment institution passported into Spain. An offshore provider without EU authorization, passporting, or an appropriately authorized local establishment cannot lawfully provide regulated payment or e-money services to the Spanish SL merely through a foreign website. EMI funds are safeguarded and are not equivalent to insured bank deposits. Availability of local Spanish IBANs, beneficiary-name matching, SEPA Instant access, SWIFT capability, client-money segregation, safeguarding disclosures, account statements, and tax-audit support must be verified. Stripe and Paddle may support collection and merchant settlement but do not replace a principal operating bank account, and their reserves, rolling holds, chargeback procedures, prohibited-business rules, and settlement-country restrictions must be incorporated into liquidity planning.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Non-resident shareholder or director with no Spanish tax identification number, incomplete identification, or inconsistent names across passports, corporate records, and bank forms.

Root cause: Non-resident shareholder or director with no Spanish tax identification number, incomplete identification, or inconsistent names across passports, corporate records, and bank forms.

Defense evidence: Current passport or national identity document; Spanish NIF/NIE where required; certified proof of residential address; notarized powers of attorney; corporate registry extracts; apostilled or legalized documents where required; certified translations; and a signed identity-matching schedule explaining name variations.
Opaque ownership chain, nominee shareholder, trust arrangement, bearer-like control, or inability to identify the ultimate beneficial owner.

Root cause: Opaque ownership chain, nominee shareholder, trust arrangement, bearer-like control, or inability to identify the ultimate beneficial owner.

Defense evidence: Complete ownership chart through every intermediate entity to each natural-person beneficial owner; registry extracts for all entities; shareholder registers; constitutional documents; declarations of beneficial ownership; board resolutions; trust or foundation documents where relevant; and evidence of control rights.
Foreign inbound capital described only as 'investment' or 'loan' without a legally consistent instrument and commercial rationale.

Root cause: Foreign inbound capital described only as 'investment' or 'loan' without a legally consistent instrument and commercial rationale.

Defense evidence: Executed subscription or shareholder-loan agreement; board and shareholder approvals; source-of-funds evidence; originating bank statements; capitalization table; transfer-pricing analysis for related-party debt; repayment and interest terms; applicable foreign-investment declarations; and a payment instruction identifying the precise legal purpose.
Expected activity inconsistent with a newly incorporated SEO, content analytics, or MarTech SaaS company, including high-volume pass-through payments, cash activity, cryptocurrency flows, or unexplained third-party collections.

Root cause: Expected activity inconsistent with a newly incorporated SEO, content analytics, or MarTech SaaS company, including high-volume pass-through payments, cash activity, cryptocurrency flows, or unexplained third-party collections.

Defense evidence: Business plan; product demonstrations; website and terms of service; customer segmentation; signed customer contracts; invoices; Stripe and Paddle agreements; forecast transaction volumes and countries; payroll and supplier budgets; source-of-revenue schedule; and a written funds-flow map distinguishing customer receipts, refunds, taxes, payroll, suppliers, and shareholder funding.
Payments involving sanctioned jurisdictions, politically exposed persons, high-risk countries, privacy-enhancing cryptocurrency services, or counterparties with adverse media.

Root cause: Payments involving sanctioned jurisdictions, politically exposed persons, high-risk countries, privacy-enhancing cryptocurrency services, or counterparties with adverse media.

Defense evidence: Counterparty due-diligence file; sanctions-screening results; beneficial-owner verification; contract and invoice; end-use statement; shipping or service-delivery evidence; adverse-media resolution memorandum; compliance approval; and documented prohibition of transactions that cannot be cleared under EU, Spanish, UN, or applicable US sanctions.
Large or repeated transfers between the Spanish SL and related parties lacking arm's-length pricing or supporting services.

Root cause: Large or repeated transfers between the Spanish SL and related parties lacking arm's-length pricing or supporting services.

Defense evidence: Intercompany agreements; transfer-pricing master and local-file support where applicable; service descriptions; time records; deliverables; comparable pricing; withholding-tax analysis; VAT analysis; board approvals; invoices; and evidence that the recipient performed the stated services.
Use of a virtual office, registered-office address, residential address, or Spanish company with no apparent local management or economic activity.

Root cause: Use of a virtual office, registered-office address, residential address, or Spanish company with no apparent local management or economic activity.

Defense evidence: Lease or serviced-office agreement; employee or contractor records; director-residency and management explanation; customer and supplier contracts; Spanish tax registrations; accounting records; operational calendar; local service-provider agreements; and a written substance and governance memorandum.
Frequent foreign-currency conversions, unexplained transfers to personal accounts, or payment flows that bypass the principal corporate account.

Root cause: Frequent foreign-currency conversions, unexplained transfers to personal accounts, or payment flows that bypass the principal corporate account.

Defense evidence: Treasury policy; approved bank-account matrix; dual-authorization controls; monthly bank reconciliations; foreign-exchange policy; board-approved intercompany payment procedures; payroll records; expense policy; and transaction-level invoices and approvals.
Incomplete tax, accounting, or beneficial-ownership filings, including inconsistencies between bank information, Agencia Tributaria records, commercial registry data, and annual accounts.

Root cause: Incomplete tax, accounting, or beneficial-ownership filings, including inconsistencies between bank information, Agencia Tributaria records, commercial registry data, and annual accounts.

Defense evidence: Current tax registration certificates; filed corporate-tax and VAT returns where available; annual accounts; commercial-registry extract; beneficial-ownership information; accountant confirmation; reconciliation of registered activities and bank activity; and remediation evidence for any historical discrepancy.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Route shareholder equity, share-premium funding, or shareholder loans from an account held in the verified name of the investor directly to the Spanish SL's account at an EU-regulated bank. Use SEPA Credit Transfer for euro funding and SWIFT MT103 for non-SEPA currencies or banks. The payment reference should identify the Spanish SL, investor, legal instrument, and purpose, such as 'share capital contribution', 'share premium contribution', or 'shareholder loan under agreement dated [date]'. Avoid third-party funding, cash deposits, unexplained payment intermediaries, and personal accounts. Before receipt, provide the bank with the subscription or loan agreement, corporate approvals, ownership chart, source-of-funds evidence, expected amount and currency, and beneficial-owner information. The bank should verify the originating account, sanctions status, source and purpose of funds, and whether any foreign-investment or statistical declaration is required. Convert currencies through the bank or an authorized EU investment-services or payment provider under documented treasury limits. Record the transaction in the general ledger, reconcile the bank credit, and retain the SWIFT or SEPA confirmation, exchange-rate evidence, and supporting corporate documentation.Use SEPA Credit Transfer or SEPA Instant for euro payments to EU suppliers where available. Use SWIFT MT103 for international supplier, contractor, tax, and service payments outside SEPA. For documentary trade, use an irrevocable documentary letter of credit subject to UCP 600, preferably confirmed where country or bank risk warrants, and require compliant commercial invoices, transport documents, insurance documents, packing lists, certificates of origin, and inspection documents. Use documentary collections under URC 522 where a lower-cost alternative is commercially acceptable. For service and SaaS payments, retain the contract, invoice, proof of performance, VAT treatment, withholding-tax assessment, and beneficiary verification. For exports, retain customs declarations, transport evidence, customer order, invoice, delivery evidence, and VAT support. Establish dual approval, beneficiary call-back verification, segregation of duties, sanctions screening, invoice-fraud controls, payment limits, and a documented exception process. MT103 is a payment message and does not itself prove trade compliance; the commercial and customs dossier must be retained separately.Deliverable forward exchange contracts with an authorized bank or regulated investment firm, used to hedge documented forecast or contracted euro and foreign-currency exposures and supported by an approved treasury policy.Non-deliverable forwards where the relevant currency is non-deliverable or local regulation prevents physical settlement; settlement should occur in the agreed convertible currency and be supported by the underlying exposure and counterparty documentation.Currency swaps or cross-currency interest-rate swaps for documented recurring cash-flow or debt exposures, subject to counterparty credit limits, collateral terms, valuation controls, and applicable EU derivatives requirements.Plain-vanilla foreign-exchange swaps for short-term liquidity management and settlement-date mismatches, subject to documented commercial purpose and authorized-counterparty controls.Foreign-exchange options or collars where the company accepts premium, valuation, accounting, and suitability risks and the instrument is proportionate to the underlying exposure.Hedging with an EU-authorized bank or investment firm must comply with applicable MiFID II conduct requirements, EMIR obligations where applicable, derivatives reporting and risk-mitigation rules, contractual netting and collateral documentation, and internal limits. Speculative trading, leveraged products without a documented exposure, and transactions with unregulated counterparties should be prohibited.

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Medium to High for payment collection, card expenditure, SEPA transfers, and multi-currency treasury where the provider is an EU-authorized electronic-money institution or payment institution passported into Spain. An offshore provider without EU authorization, passporting, or an appropriately authorized local establishment cannot lawfully provide regulated payment or e-money services to the Spanish SL merely through a foreign website. EMI funds are safeguarded and are not equivalent to insured bank deposits. Availability of local Spanish IBANs, beneficiary-name matching, SEPA Instant access, SWIFT capability, client-money segregation, safeguarding disclosures, account statements, and tax-audit support must be verified. Stripe and Paddle may support collection and merchant settlement but do not replace a principal operating bank account, and their reserves, rolling holds, chargeback procedures, prohibited-business rules, and settlement-country restrictions must be incorporated into liquidity planning.

Stage 06

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25% general Spanish Corporate Income Tax rate. Newly incorporated entities may apply 15% during the first profitable tax period and the following tax period, subject to statutory eligibility and anti-abuse conditions. Qualifying newly created innovative start-ups may also apply 15%. Additional reduced rates may apply to qualifying microenterprises and other specifically regulated entities.

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% Spanish withholding tax is generally applicable to dividends paid by a Spanish SL to a non-resident. The domestic participation exemption for qualifying EU or European Economic Area corporate parent companies may eliminate withholding where the statutory conditions are satisfied, including qualifying legal form and subject-to-tax requirements, at least 10% direct or indirect participation, and the minimum holding-period requirement or undertaking. A treaty may reduce the rate, commonly to 0%, 5%, 10% or 15%, depending on the treaty and ownership conditions.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

Modelo 200 is due within the 25 calendar days following the six-month period after the end of the tax period. For a calendar-year company ending on 31 December, the normal filing and payment window is 1 to 25 July of the following year, subject to the applicable electronic-filing calendar. Modelo 202 is generally due from 1 to 20 April, 1 to 20 October and 1 to 20 December.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Normally 1 to 20 April, 1 to 20 October and 1 to 20 December. Payment by direct debit normally requires an earlier statutory banking instruction deadline.

Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: Spain generally exempts formal related-party documentation where the aggregate value of related-party transactions with the same person or entity does not exceed EUR 250,000 at arm's-length value during the tax period, subject to exclusions and special rules. Documentation requirements may apply by transaction category at lower thresholds, particularly for transactions involving real estate, intangible assets, tax jurisdictions listed under Spanish anti-abuse rules and certain business transfers. A Spanish entity forming part of a multinational group may require a Local File and Master File under the Spanish Corporate Income Tax regulations. Country-by-Country reporting generally applies to qualifying multinational groups with consolidated revenue of at least EUR 750 million.

Economic substance scope: Spain does not operate a standalone Cayman-style Economic Substance Regulation regime for ordinary Spanish SLs. Substance is nevertheless relevant through the general anti-abuse rule, simulated-transaction doctrine, beneficial-ownership requirements, treaty anti-abuse standards, controlled foreign company rules, EU anti-hybrid rules, interest-limitation rules and the principal-purpose test in applicable treaties. The SL should maintain genuine Spanish management, personnel or outsourced operational capacity, premises or demonstrable business infrastructure, decision-making records, customer and supplier contracts, functional risk control, IP and data governance, and accounting evidence proportionate to its SEO analytics SaaS activity.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Corporate Income Tax evasion and fraudulent tax return

Statutory sanction: Ordinary tax fraud may constitute a criminal offense where the evaded tax exceeds EUR 120,000 for the relevant tax period and tax. Sanctions generally include imprisonment of 1 to 5 years and a fine of 1 to 6 times the amount defrauded, together with payment of the tax, interest and civil liability. Aggravated cases, including amounts exceeding EUR 600,000 or specified organized or fraudulent conduct, may attract imprisonment of 2 to 6 years and a fine of 2 to 6 times the amount defrauded.

Director personal liability: Directors and de facto managers may incur criminal liability, civil restitution, fines, disqualification from public office or management, and subsidiary liability for tax debts where statutory requirements are met. Travel restrictions or other precautionary measures may be imposed by judicial authorities; imprisonment is possible in criminal cases.
False invoicing, sham services and transfer-pricing manipulation

Statutory sanction: Tax adjustments may increase the taxable base and trigger late-payment interest and penalties generally ranging from 50% to 150% of the unpaid tax depending on concealment, fraud and aggravating circumstances. False invoices may also constitute accounting or tax crimes where criminal thresholds and intent requirements are satisfied.

Director personal liability: Directors approving fictitious or unsupported transactions may face civil liability to the company, tax derivation, criminal liability for fraud or accounting offenses, disqualification and personal fines. Corporate veil protection does not shield deliberate fraud or unlawful asset extraction.
Failure to withhold or remit non-resident tax

Statutory sanction: The Spanish SL may be assessed for the unwithheld tax, late-payment interest and withholding penalties. Penalties depend on the nature and severity of the omission and may generally reach 50% to 150% of the unpaid amount where a tax infringement is established.

Director personal liability: Directors may face subsidiary tax liability or civil claims where they caused or tolerated the failure and statutory derivation conditions are satisfied. Deliberate concealment, falsification or repeated evasion may create criminal exposure.
Shell company, treaty abuse and lack of economic substance

Statutory sanction: The AEAT may deny treaty or EU directive relief, recharacterize transactions, apply withholding and Corporate Income Tax adjustments, impose interest and penalties, and invoke Spain's general anti-abuse and simulated-transaction rules. Benefits may be denied even where formal documentation exists.

Director personal liability: Directors and beneficial owners may face tax derivation, civil damages, disqualification and criminal exposure where sham conduct, money laundering or tax fraud is proven. The corporate form does not protect persons using the SL as an artificial conduit.
Accounting and corporate-record falsification

Statutory sanction: Consequences include tax reassessment, accounting and tax penalties, rejection of deductible costs, possible commercial-law sanctions and criminal accounting-document offenses where statutory elements are met.

Director personal liability: Directors, finance officers and persons authorizing false records may incur personal criminal, civil and tax liability, including disqualification and restitution.
Anti-money laundering and beneficial-ownership failure

Statutory sanction: Under Spanish AML legislation, serious infringements may attract fines generally from EUR 60,000 to EUR 150,000 per infringement, while very serious infringements may attract fines from EUR 150,000 to EUR 5 million or up to 10% of annual turnover, subject to statutory limits and aggravating factors. Additional public reprimands, authorization restrictions and management disqualification may apply.

Director personal liability: Responsible directors and officers may receive personal fines, temporary disqualification and other administrative sanctions. Knowing participation in laundering may constitute a criminal offense carrying imprisonment, fines and asset confiscation; precautionary travel restrictions may be ordered in judicial proceedings.
Failure to maintain Spanish books, records and supporting evidence

Statutory sanction: The tax authority may reject deductions, estimate the tax base, impose record-keeping and obstruction penalties, assess unpaid tax and interest, and apply broader tax penalties where the missing evidence conceals taxable income.

Director personal liability: Directors may face civil and tax liability if the record failure is deliberate, obstructive or part of fraudulent conduct. Routine negligence generally creates corporate rather than automatic personal liability, subject to statutory derivation rules.
Improper profit distribution and unlawful asset extraction

Statutory sanction: Distributions may be repayable, related-party payments may be recharacterized as dividends or remuneration, and tax, interest and penalties may apply. Spanish Companies Law remedies may include restitution, director liability and shareholder claims.

Director personal liability: Directors may be jointly liable for unlawful distributions, corporate losses and creditor damage where statutory duties are breached. Fraudulent extraction may additionally support insolvency, civil and criminal proceedings.
